name: Acitretin
lead: Acitretin is an oral second-generation retinoid used for severe psoriasis that has not responded to other treatments, and off-label for several disorders of keratinisation.[1][2] It is the active metabolite of etretinate and is sold under brand names including Soriatane and Neotigason.[1] It is a prescription-only drug in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.[1]

Its relevance to appearance is as a treatment for visible skin disease rather than as a cosmetic. Its best-known risk is severe teratogenicity: the labelling and reviews require strict pregnancy prevention during treatment and for years afterwards.[1][2] Common side effects resemble vitamin A excess, including dry skin and lips and hair loss.[1][2]

paras: Acitretin is indicated for severe psoriasis in adults, including pustular and erythrodermic forms, and is generally reserved for refractory cases rather than mild or moderate disease.[1][2] Off-label uses described include Darier disease, lamellar ichthyosis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen planus, palmoplantar pustulosis and prevention of non-melanoma skin cancer in high-risk patients such as organ-transplant recipients.[2] Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology and the National Psoriasis Foundation, and European guidelines, list acitretin among traditional systemic psoriasis therapies.[3][4][5]

Wikipedia lists nausea, headache, itching, dry or flaky skin, dry or red eyes, dry or swollen lips, thirst, and hair loss as common effects.[1] Grokipedia adds hypertriglyceridaemia, musculoskeletal pain, and, more rarely, hepatotoxicity, pseudotumor cerebri and pancreatitis, and notes that liver function and lipids are monitored during treatment.[2]

Acitretin is highly teratogenic, with risks including malformations of the face, skull, spine, limbs and ears.[1] It is not for use in pregnancy, and guidance calls for two forms of contraception and avoidance of pregnancy for about three years after stopping, partly because acitretin can be converted back to etretinate in the body.[1][2]

Acitretin acts on nuclear retinoic acid and retinoid X receptors, which regulate gene transcription and promote normal keratinocyte differentiation while reducing epidermal overgrowth.[1][2] Oral bioavailability is roughly 60 percent, protein binding exceeds 99.9 percent, and the elimination half-life is about 49 hours.[1] Clinical improvement is typically described as emerging over weeks to a few months.[1][2]

Roche patented acitretin in Germany in 1974, and it was approved in the United States in 1996.[1] It succeeded etretinate, whose very long half-life and teratogenic potential led to its withdrawal.[1][6]

A double-blind, placebo-controlled study in renal transplant recipients examined acitretin for skin-cancer prevention and reduction of keratotic lesions.[7] Registered trials have examined acitretin in severe plaque psoriasis (dose-ranging, n=61), nail psoriasis (n=36), combination with etanercept in psoriasis (n=10 and n=60), chronic hand dermatitis (n=9), HIV-associated psoriasis (n=30) and hidradenitis suppurativa versus apremilast (n=70, 2024); several others were withdrawn or terminated.[8][9][10][11][12][13] Reviews report PASI 75 responses of roughly one-third to one-half of patients at 12 weeks in psoriasis trials.[2] No studies were found of acitretin for purely cosmetic purposes.

timeline.event: Acitretin patented in Germany by Roche.[1]

card.summary: A prescription oral retinoid for severe psoriasis and keratinisation disorders, with strict pregnancy-prevention rules.
card.note: Highly teratogenic; contraception required during and for about three years after treatment.

quick.overview:
Acitretin is an oral vitamin A-derived drug prescribed for severe psoriasis and certain disorders where skin thickens and scales abnormally.

It is a treatment for skin disease, not an established cosmetic; studies of purely cosmetic use were not found.
quick.mechanism: It binds nuclear retinoid receptors and shifts gene activity so skin cells mature normally and over-multiply less. Its half-life is about two days.
quick.risks: Documented risks include severe birth defects, dry skin and lips, hair loss, raised blood fats and rare liver problems. It is prescription-only, with pregnancy prevention required for about three years after use.
